645.title: Kumbhakarna
645.hook: Ravana loses his first duel, and orders the giant who sleeps for months to be woken
645.carry: only reached for when he's losing
645.howItsDone: The waking of Kumbhakarna is a favorite scene in Ramlila and in shadow-puppet traditions, often played for laughs before his serious conversation with Ravana.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Garuda's old story. Two sisters, a cheat, a son who freed his mother, and the bird who carries Vishnu. A friend on the wind.

Ravana finally rides out himself. He strikes Lakshmana down with a great dart and tries to lift him to carry him off, and can't move him. Hanuman can, easily, and carries Lakshmana to safety. Then Rama meets Ravana, smashes his chariot, and cuts the crown from his head. And Rama stops. You've fought hard today, he says, and you're tired. Go home and rest. Come back tomorrow, and see what I can do. Ravana goes home alive, beaten, humiliated. And he gives an order: wake my brother.
screen: `RAVANA RIDES OUT.` → `GO HOME AND REST.` → `WAKE MY BROTHER.`

segments.voice: Ravana's brother is Kumbhakarna, and his name says it: pot-ears. He's a giant beyond giants, and he sleeps. Not for a night. For months. Waking him is a comic set piece in the war book, and Valmiki enjoys it. Rakshasas pile up mountains of food beside him, meat and rice and great jars to drink. They beat drums and blow conches by his ears. They shout, hit him with clubs and hammers, and march elephants over his body. Nothing. Finally he yawns, stretches, and wakes up hungry. Why does he sleep like that? Valmiki gives two answers in different places. In the Yuddha Kanda, Vibhishana tells Rama that the young Kumbhakarna devoured creatures without limit, and Brahma, the creator, cursed him to sleep as if dead. Ravana begged for mercy, so Brahma softened it: six months asleep, then a single day awake. In the Uttara Kanda it goes differently. As Kumbhakarna was about to ask Brahma for a boon, the gods feared what he'd ask, so the goddess Sarasvati entered his speech, and the boon he asked for was sleep. Later tellers added a pun: he meant to ask for Indra's throne, indrasana, and the word came out nidrasana, the seat of sleep. Notice the shape of it. Ravana has left this giant asleep through the war so far, and he only reaches for him when he's losing.
screen: `KUMBHAKARNA: POT-EARS.` · `DRUMS, CLUBS AND ELEPHANTS.` · `A CURSE, OR A TWISTED BOON.` · `INDRASANA BECOMES NIDRASANA.` · then, large: `WOKEN ONLY WHEN RAVANA IS LOSING.`

segments.voice: Let yourself be heavy, like a sleeper, and feel your weight in the chair or on the floor. Then look in gently, the way you'd check on someone sleeping, at a strength in you that only wakes when things go wrong, and let it stir with the breath.
Kumbhakarna. Ravana's giant brother, pot-ears, who sleeps for months under a curse or a twisted boon, woken only now that Ravana is losing.
Your line: only reached for when he's losing. Awake now, the giant has something to tell his brother. Day six hundred forty-five.

646.title: Kumbhakarna
646.hook: the giant tells his brother he's wrong, and goes to fight for him anyway
646.carry: clear about right, bound by love
646.howItsDone: Kumbhakarna's rebuke of Ravana and his loyalty are much discussed in Ramayana storytelling, and Kamban's Tamil scene of the two brothers, Vibhishana and Kumbhakarna, meeting on the battlefield is often recited.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kumbhakarna, the giant who sleeps for months, woken with drums and elephants because Ravana was losing. Only reached for when he's losing.

Kumbhakarna walks into Ravana's hall, still huge with sleep, and Ravana pours it all out. Rama has crossed the sea. Our best warriors are dead. I lost today. You're the only one left who can save us. The court waits for the giant's roar. And Kumbhakarna, the brother known for sleeping and eating, says what only Vibhishana has said to the king's face, and Vibhishana was driven out for it.
screen: `RAVANA POURS IT OUT.` → `YOU'RE THE ONLY ONE LEFT.` → `THE GIANT SPEAKS PLAINLY.`

segments.voice: We told you, he says. At your council, this is exactly what we said would happen. A king who acts first and thinks afterward, who does what he wants and ignores good advice, brings disaster on himself. You took another man's wife. This is the result. Ravana's face darkens. He wants a champion, not a lecture. And Kumbhakarna sees his brother hurting, and softens. Enough, he says. Don't grieve. Whatever you did, I'm your brother. I'll go and kill your enemy. That's the knot at his heart. He knows Ravana is wrong, says so to his face, and goes to fight for him anyway, out of loyalty. On the battlefield he's terrifying. The monkeys scatter, and Angada has to shame them into turning back. He seizes Sugriva and carries him off under his arm toward the city. Sugriva comes to his senses, tears at the giant's ears and nose, and escapes. In the end Rama faces him and brings him down with his arrows, and Valmiki says the great head fell on Lanka. The Tamil poet Kamban adds a scene. Before the fight, Vibhishana comes to his brother on the field and begs him to join Rama. Kumbhakarna refuses gently. You did right, he says, more or less; you stay with Rama. My place is with our brother. Some readers see a fool here. Others see an honest man: clear about what is right, and bound by love to what is wrong.

segments.voice: Recall a time loyalty pulled you one way and your sense of right pulled another, and don't judge the person you were. Breathe with both pulls side by side, the way Kumbhakarna carried them, and let the knot loosen a little.

647.title: Lakshmana wounded
647.hook: Lakshmana's greatest victory, and the same day, Indrajit comes back with Brahma's weapon
647.carry: the strength to accept a blow
647.howItsDone: Ramayana tellers often present Rama's choice to endure Brahma's weapon as respect for the creator's power, and set it beside the serpent-arrows earlier in the war.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kumbhakarna told Ravana plainly he was wrong, then fought for him anyway, and fell. Clear about right, bound by love.

With Kumbhakarna gone, Ravana sends out his other sons. One of them, Atikaya, is a giant in armor that Brahma himself gave him, and no arrow will go through it. Lakshmana fights him a long time, getting nowhere. Then, Valmiki says, the wind god Vayu comes close and whispers in Lakshmana's ear: that armor came from Brahma. Only Brahma's own weapon will break it. Lakshmana takes the hint, and Atikaya falls. It's Lakshmana's great victory. It doesn't last the day.
screen: `ATIKAYA IN BRAHMA'S ARMOR.` → `THE WIND WHISPERS.` → `LAKSHMANA'S GREAT VICTORY.`

segments.voice: Indrajit comes back. Several of his brothers, his uncle Kumbhakarna and a string of champions are dead, and he's furious. This time he prepares. Before he rides out, he makes offerings into a sacred fire, and he comes out with a chariot that can't be seen. Then, from out of sight again, he invokes the weapon of Brahma, the creator. It isn't one arrow. It's a storm. Valmiki pictures the whole field covered: Sugriva, Angada, Jambavan, Nila, leader after leader falling, the monkey army brought down in vast numbers. And Rama does something surprising. He knows what this weapon is, and he chooses not to fight it. This is Brahma's weapon, he tells Lakshmana; it deserves respect. Let's endure it. So the two brothers stand in the rain of arrows and fall, Rama and then Lakshmana, side by side once again. Indrajit rides home to Lanka in triumph. Notice the difference from the first time. With the serpent-arrows, the brothers were taken by surprise. This time Rama sees it coming and lets it strike, because he won't treat the creator's power as if it were nothing. It's a strange kind of strength, the strength to accept a blow. The battlefield is left at night, quiet, strewn with the fallen. Somewhere among them, a few are still awake.
screen: `INDRAJIT'S FIRE OFFERING.` · `THE WEAPON OF BRAHMA.` · `RAMA CHOOSES TO ENDURE IT.` · `THE BROTHERS FALL AGAIN.` · then, large: `THE STRENGTH TO ACCEPT A BLOW.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you can't fight right now, an illness, a loss, a choice someone else made, and stop bracing against it for these few breaths. Soften the shoulders as you breathe in and the jaw as you breathe out; accepting isn't the same as giving up.

648.title: Lakshmana wounded
648.hook: two torches crossing a battlefield at night, and an old bear's surprising question
648.howItsDone: Devotees of Hanuman often retell Jambavan's question, is Hanuman alive, as a sign of Hanuman's place in the Ramayana.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama and Lakshmana chose to endure Brahma's weapon, and fell with much of the army. The strength to accept a blow.

Two people are still on their feet: Vibhishana, who knows the weapons of Lanka, and Hanuman. It's night. They take torches and walk out across the battlefield, stepping between fallen warriors, looking for anyone still alive. Rama and Lakshmana lie in the arrows. Leader after leader lies still. Then, in the torchlight, they find Jambavan, the old king of the bears, so pierced with arrows he can't open his eyes, still breathing.
screen: `TWO STILL STANDING.` → `TORCHES ACROSS THE FIELD.` → `JAMBAVAN, STILL BREATHING.`

segments.voice: Vibhishana kneels and asks if he's alive. Jambavan knows the voice, though he can't see. And his first question isn't about Rama, or Lakshmana, or Sugriva his king. It's this: is Hanuman alive? Vibhishana is puzzled. Why Hanuman, and not the princes? Jambavan's answer is short and startling. If Hanuman lives, the whole army lives, even if it has been killed. If Hanuman is dead, we're dead, though we're still breathing. Hanuman steps forward and bows at the old bear's feet. Jambavan, revived by the sound of him, gives his orders. Go north, over the ocean, to the Himalaya. Between Mount Rishabha and Mount Kailasa is a mountain covered with healing herbs. He names four. One that brings back life. One that draws out arrows. One that restores the body's color. One that joins what's broken. Bring them back, and the army will rise. Why ask about Hanuman first? One way to read it: he's thinking like an elder. Who can still act tonight? Who can cross a sea and come back before dawn? Grief would ask about the princes. Wisdom asks about the one who can save them. And it was Jambavan, you may remember, who once reminded Hanuman of his own strength before the great leap to Lanka. Now, on a dark field, he does it again.

segments.voice: Take a hard situation around you, at home or at work, and set aside for a moment whose fault it is or who is hurt most. Breathe slowly, and ask Jambavan's question instead: who can still act?

649.title: the mountain of herbs
649.hook: a night flight the length of India, and herbs that hide
649.howItsDone: Images of Hanuman flying with a mountain on his hand are found in temples, homes and calendars across India, and many Hindus pray to him in times of illness.

segments.voice: Yesterday: on a dark field, Jambavan asked first whether Hanuman was alive, and sent him north for four healing herbs. Is Hanuman alive.

Hanuman climbs a mountain at the edge of the sea to push off, and he grows, the way he grew before the first leap. He presses down with his feet, and the mountain buckles under him. Then he's in the air, heading north. This isn't the hop to Lanka. This is the whole length of India, there and back, before dawn, with the army lying in the dark behind him.

Valmiki lets us ride along. Below him slide the ocean, then forests, rivers and towns, the hermitages of sages, the land unrolling under a flying monkey at night. Then the Himalaya rise ahead, snow and gold and rock. He sees Kailasa, the home of Shiva. He sees Mount Rishabha. And between them, just as Jambavan said, the mountain of herbs, glowing with its plants. Then the twist. Hanuman searches the slopes, and he can't find the four herbs. Valmiki says the plants knew someone had come for them, and hid; they made themselves invisible. You've crossed half the world, the clock is running, and the thing you came for won't let itself be found. Hanuman won't spend the rest of the night searching. He gets angry, and speaks to the mountain. You won't help Rama? Then see what happens. He grips the whole peak, with its trees, its animals, its glowing herbs, tears it loose, and lifts it into the sky. He flies south with it, Valmiki says, shining like a second sun. If you've grown up seeing Hanuman's picture, this is the one: a monkey in flight, a mountain held up on one hand. It began with a plant that wouldn't be found, and a messenger who decided not to choose. If I can't find the one thing, he reasons, I'll bring everything.

650.title: the mountain of herbs
650.hook: the smell of a mountain on the wind, an army rising, and a peak put back
650.howItsDone: Hanuman's flight with the herb mountain is recited and sung in devotion to him, in Valmiki's telling and in later ones such as the Ramcharitmanas.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mountain of herbs. The plants hid, so Hanuman lifted the whole peak and flew it south like a second sun.

The monkeys still conscious see it first: a light in the northern sky, coming fast. Then they hear Hanuman's roar, and they roar back, weak and astonished. He sets down over the battlefield with a mountain in his hands, trees and rocks and all, glowing in the dark. And before anyone has picked a single leaf, something happens that nobody planned. The wind carries the scent of the herbs out over the field.
screen: `A LIGHT IN THE NORTH.` → `HANUMAN'S ROAR.` → `THE SCENT ON THE WIND.`

segments.voice: In Valmiki, that's all it takes. The smell of the herbs drifts over the fallen, and they rise. Rama and Lakshmana breathe in, the arrows come out of them, and their wounds close. All around them the monkeys and bears get up, shaking themselves as if they'd been asleep. Valmiki goes further: even monkeys who had been killed come back to life. He notes something about the other side, too. The rakshasas who had died didn't rise, because Ravana had ordered his dead thrown into the sea, so the enemy wouldn't see how many he'd lost. A king hiding his losses, and so cutting his own people off from healing: Valmiki lets that detail speak for itself. Then Hanuman does something the famous picture doesn't show. He picks up the mountain again, flies it all the way back north, sets it in its place in the Himalaya, and returns to the camp. The peak was borrowed, not taken. He doesn't keep the prize or put it on display. The emergency is over, so the mountain goes home. In a later telling, the Ramcharitmanas of Tulsidas, Bharata shoots Hanuman down over Ayodhya as he carries the mountain. In Valmiki the trip is uninterrupted: north, south, north again, and back before the battle starts.
screen: `THE SCENT ALONE HEALS.` · `EVEN THE FALLEN RISE.` · `RAVANA HID HIS DEAD.` · `THE MOUNTAIN GOES HOME.` · then, large: `BORROWED, NOT TAKEN.`

651.title: the mountain of herbs
651.hook: how one flight became the picture on a million walls
651.howItsDone: Devotees of Hanuman recite the Hanuman Chalisa, often on Tuesdays and Saturdays, and images of Hanuman carrying the mountain hang in homes, temples and shops; people pray to him for the recovery of the sick.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mrtasanjivani, the reviving herb. Its scent lifted the fallen army, and Hanuman carried the peak back home. Borrowed, not taken.

On a roadside shrine in North India, on the wall of a truck stop, in a grandmother's prayer room, the same picture keeps turning up: Hanuman in flight, mace in one hand, a mountain balanced on the other. Ask someone what's happening in it, and they'll probably tell a slightly different story from the one you've just heard. Lakshmana is dying. There's a physician. There's a deadline at dawn. That version is real too, and here's where it comes from.
screen: `A PICTURE ON SHRINE WALLS.` → `LAKSHMANA IS DYING.` → `A DEADLINE AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: Valmiki actually tells a herb flight twice. The first is the one you've followed: after Indrajit's Brahma weapon, the whole army down, Jambavan sending Hanuman north. The second comes near the very end of the war, when Lakshmana alone is struck by a spear, and Sushena, the monkey physician, sends Hanuman for the herbs again. Over time, in popular memory, the two have flowed together into one: Lakshmana wounded, the physician, the flight, the mountain, the race against the dawn. Later poets shaped that memory too. The Hanuman Chalisa, a hymn to Hanuman that devotees recite, often on Tuesdays and Saturdays, says it in one line: he brought the life-giving herb, and Lakshmana lived, and Rama embraced him with joy. For some people that line is the whole story, even if they've never opened Valmiki. So which is right? Both are part of the tradition. Valmiki keeps the two rescues apart. The devotional tradition keeps the heart of it: Hanuman as the one who brings healing, against the clock, when everyone else is helpless. It's one reason people pray to him when someone they love is in hospital. And so a week closes that ran from a giant woken with drums, through a brother who fought for a brother he knew was wrong, to Lakshmana's great victory and great fall, an old bear's question in the dark, and a mountain flying south.
